A map value is a handle to a shared table, so copying a map shares its entries; the zero value of a map type is nil, and a literal is what makes it non-nil.

complexity_detail.description: The index expression `a[x]` means different things by operand type: a bounds-checked element of an array/slice/string, or a total map lookup that yields the zero value for an absent key.

complexity_detail.description: Exception to addressability: map elements are NOT addressable, although array and slice elements are, so `&m[k]` is rejected and a map element cannot be updated in place through a reference.

probes.support_reason: Deterministic tie-break, all-yes, so FULL under F-1..F-4 and F-6. The measured fragment is the complete function declaration and body, as the probe's measured_fragment requires. (1) `os.Open("data.txt")` opens the named file for reading using only the standard library and can fail, which the written `err` result makes explicit. (2) `io.ReadAll(f)` reads the entire contents and `text := string(b)` binds them to a text-string local named `text`. (3) `defer f.Close()` is Go's normal scoped-cleanup mechanism and guarantees the handle is released when the enclosing function scope ends INCLUDING when step (2) fails - spec 'Defer statements': 'deferred functions are executed ... immediately before the surrounding function returns'. VERIFIED, not asserted: an instrumented copy in which the reader returns an error from Read (the read-failure path) reports `closed= true`, so the release happens on the failure path too; transcript recorded in the diagnostics field. (4) `return len(text), nil` returns the length in bytes of `text` (`len` of a string is its byte count, spec 'Length and capacity'), and both failure paths propagate the error to the caller through the declared `error` result, which is the way Go's mechanism requires. F-2/F-3/F-4: only `os`, `io` and core language; builds and runs under the frozen recipe `go build -o BIN FILE.go` with data.txt = 'hello\n'; stdout '6'. F-6: neither `os.Open`, `io.ReadAll` nor `(*os.File).Close` carries a sentence of normative prohibition or deprecation in its documentation. R10 SELECTION RECORD: (a) THE MEASURED FORM = 70 tokens; (b) dropping the second error check and writing `return len(text), err` = 60 tokens - REJECTED under R2, which forbids golfing: it returns a non-zero length alongside a non-nil error, and the cross-language equivalent this benchmark measures (Rust's `io::read_to_string(&file)?`) returns without a length on the error path, so the 60-token form is not the same observable behaviour on that path (authoring rule R1.1.3 fragment equivalence). The rejected form is recorded here so a reviewer can flip the decision mechanically. (c) `os.ReadFile("data.txt")` = 44 tokens - REJECTED because it delivers no handle and therefore no sub-requirement (1) or (3) at all.

Axes: A2 = the file system and the file's read offset, both outside the fragment, are touched; A6 = may yield an error VALUE that the fragment binds and tests and that the signature hands to the caller (never a throw, never a trap); A7 = the target of each call is a package-level function or a method on a concrete pointer type, fixed once the package is fixed; A8 = an OS resource is acquired at statement 1, a heap buffer at statement 4, a second heap copy at statement 6, and the resource is RELEASED at function exit; A9 = may return early, twice. WITNESS: the frozen probe file, built with `go build -o BIN main.go` under the frozen semantic_compression recipe, data.txt = 'hello\n'; observer output '6'.

V2 - the rebound-import reading. `os` and `io` are single identifiers whose binding is an IMPORT DECLARATION OUTSIDE the measured fragment, which methodology 03 Rule 1.1.2 makes external, and Go import declarations may rename a package to any identifier (Go 1.26 Language Specification, 'Import declarations': 'If an explicit period (.) appears instead of a name, ... Otherwise ... the identifier ... is used'). The same 70 tokens are equally compatible with `os` and `io` naming user packages, in which case NO file is opened, NO descriptor is acquired or released at the `defer`, nothing outside the process is touched, and the byte length returned is whatever those packages produce. Materially different on A2 (no external side effect), A6 (a different failure domain) and A8 (no OS resource event at all). locality_detail.required_for_fact: possible_failure, externally_visible_side_effects and allocation_copy_move_borrow_destroy. Reading `Open`'s contract resolves all three at class level in one hop: that the call can fail and how (an `error` of type *PathError), that it performs OS I/O and opens a file with mode O_RDONLY, and that an OS resource is acquired. Chosen first by the greedy rule of methodology 03 section 2.3 step 7 because it resolves the largest number of unresolved facts. Standard-library declarations are hops on the same terms as user declarations (methodology 03 Rule 2.2.2), even though methodology 02 section 2.2 admits this same consultation into Semantic Density's COUNT test - the declared divergence of methodology 02 section 2.3.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H3 - Overload or dynamic dispatch not locally evident
hidden_items.why: Local site 1, `f, err := os.Open("data.txt")`. `os` is a package name bound by an import declaration written OUTSIDE the measured fragment, which methodology 04 section 0.7 excludes from the local site ('imported definitions' and 'declarations of names used by the site but written elsewhere'). Under Go 1.26 Language Specification, 'Import declarations' an import may bind ANY identifier to any package path, so the set of candidate bodies compatible with this site has cardinality >= 2 and no per-candidate equivalence record exists (section 1.4.0 route). The LED gate fails because the specification does not fix which package `os` denotes. Witnessed by the determinacy witness v2_rebound_import, in which the byte-identical site calls a user package's `Open`.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H3 - Overload or dynamic dispatch not locally evident
hidden_items.why: Local site 4, `b, err := io.ReadAll(f)` - a distinct local site and therefore a distinct event under section 1.3.2. Two rules fire here and are recorded as ONE event, matching the treatment applied to the comparison languages: `io` is bound by an external import declaration, and the argument `f` has the type of a binding made at local site 1, which is not local here. Same citation as above.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H3 - Overload or dynamic dispatch not locally evident
hidden_items.why: Local site 3, `defer f.Close()` - a distinct local site. The receiver's type is fixed at local site 1, which section 0.7 excludes, so the site alone does not determine which `Close` body the deferred call will run. NOTE that Go's method call itself adds nothing here: `*os.File` is a concrete pointer type and Go has no method overriding, so the ambiguity is entirely the cross-site one.

Local site 4, the argument position of `io.ReadAll(f)`. A concrete `*os.File` is converted to the `io.Reader` INTERFACE with nothing written at the position: Go 1.26 Language Specification, 'Assignability' inserts the conversion whenever the value implements the interface. It changes the representation the callee receives from a one-word pointer to a two-word (type, value) pair and changes what operations are available to it, so it is material under section 0.8 on the representation and dispatch dimensions. Assigned to H1 rather than H7 by the single-assignment precedence of section 1.3.1. Charged at this site as a rule distinct from the H3 event above.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H4 - Implicit allocation, copy, move, destruction, or cleanup
hidden_items.why: Local site 6, `text := string(b)`. The conversion COPIES every byte into a newly allocated immutable string - it must, because `b` remains writable while strings are immutable (Go 1.26 Language Specification, 'String types' and 'Conversions to and from a string type') - and the site's only token is a CONVERSION token, which H4's exclusion list does not cover: the exclusion is for 'allocation named by a local token whose specified or demonstrated meaning is the creation of a new object or value of that type', and `string(x)` is spelled as a type conversion, not as a constructor or allocation. The copy is material on the independent-mutation and cost-class dimensions of H4's own test. Contrast local site 1 and local site 3, which are NOT charged: `os.Open` is a factory call (excluded) and `defer f.Close()` is cleanup named by a locally written scope construct plus an explicit close (excluded) - that exclusion is the LED Go earns here for writing its release point, and it is why this probe carries no H4 event for the descriptor at either end.

The Go specification defines no destructor, no finalizer and no scope-exit hook of any kind for a user-defined type; the language's only cleanup construct is the written `defer` statement, and the only reclamation hook in the standard library, `runtime.AddCleanup` (and the `runtime.SetFinalizer` it replaces), is explicitly NONDETERMINISTIC - 'The cleanup is scheduled to run at some arbitrary time after ptr becomes unreachable' and 'There is no guarantee that cleanups will run before a program exits' (pkg.go.dev/runtime@go1.26.3, AddCleanup). probes.support_reason: Deterministic tie-break, all-yes, so FULL under F-1..F-4 and F-6. (1) Two `go` statements start TWO independent goroutines, the first computing 20 and the second computing 22, using only the language's own concurrency facility - spec 'Go statements': 'A "go" statement starts the execution of a function call as an independent concurrent thread of control, or goroutine, within the same address space.' No library, no runtime entry construct and no import is required, so no async-runtime scaffold appears. (2) `sum := <-ch + <-ch` WAITS FOR BOTH: the channel is unbuffered, so each send completes only when its value is received, and two receives therefore complete only after both goroutines have run their send to completion (spec 'Channel types': 'If the capacity is zero or absent, the channel is unbuffered and communication succeeds only when both a sender and receiver are ready'). (3) `sum` is bound to the sum of the two results, 42, and `return sum` produces it. Go's goroutine is a real concurrent unit, not a single-threaded cooperative one: GOMAXPROCS defaults to the number of CPUs and the two sends can run on different OS threads, so the 'single-threaded cooperative async facility DOES count' clause of the canonical task is not the one that applies here. F-2/F-3/F-4: core language only, no import at all; builds and runs under `go build -o BIN FILE.go`, stdout '42'. F-6: no normative prohibition applies to `go`, `chan` or `make`. R10 SELECTION RECORD, all tokenized with the frozen tokenizer: (a) THE MEASURED FORM = 38 tokens, prints 42; (b) buffered channel `make(chan int, 2)` = 40 tokens - and it would WEAKEN sub-requirement (2), because with capacity 2 a send completes before any receive, so the receives would no longer be the join; (c) `sync.WaitGroup` with two result variables = 48 tokens and needs an import. Sub-test H8a fires on the TARGET-PLATFORM clause: 'For the same operand types, the outcome at the edge differs depending on ... target platform, pointer or integer width'. The operand type is written at the site as `C.int`, but cgo maps that name to whatever the target's C ABI says a C `int` is (Go 1.26 cgo documentation, `go doc cmd/cgo` / pkg.go.dev/cmd/cgo@go1.26.3), so the value at which the addition wraps is not fixed by the local form. H8's third exclusion does not rescue it: that exclusion covers variation arising 'only from which type the operands were declared to be ELSEWHERE', and here the type IS declared at the site - it is the type's WIDTH that is absent. What is NOT charged, and is a real Go result rather than an oversight: sub-test H8a does NOT fire on build mode, because Go 1.26 Language Specification, 'Integer overflow' states one outcome for every signed integer type - 'the resulting value ... is deterministically defined ... Overflow does not cause a run-time panic' - and Go's toolchain exposes no flag, mode or optimization level that changes it, which is the documented-universal route that section 1.4.0 route 1 requires; a language whose overflow behaviour differs between debug and release triggers H8a on that ground and Go does not. Sub-test H8b likewise does not fire: the form admits exactly one numeric type in this probe and the only edge class it can reach is overflow. NOTE also that H3 does not fire anywhere in this fragment - there is no call at all - and H9 does not fire, because the body reads and writes nothing outside itself.
